title: Minimum Weighted Subgraph With the Required Paths II
statement:
A tree has `n = edges.length + 1` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`. Each `edges[i] = [u_i, v_i, w_i]` joins `u_i` and `v_i` by an undirected edge of weight `w_i`.

Each `queries[j] = [src1_j, src2_j, dest_j]` names three different nodes. For that query, pick a connected part of the tree (a set of its nodes and edges that is itself a tree) in which `src1_j` can travel to `dest_j` and `src2_j` can travel to `dest_j` along the picked edges only, and make the sum of the picked edge weights as small as possible.

Return an array `answer` of the same length as `queries`, where `answer[j]` is that smallest weight sum for `queries[j]`.
constraints: src1_j, src2_j and dest_j are pairwise distinct
notes:
## Intuition

A tree joins any two nodes by exactly one simple path, so every valid choice must contain the whole path from `src1` to `dest` and the whole path from `src2` to `dest`. Their union is already connected and acyclic, so it is the answer. Walking both paths for every query costs O(n) each, too slow for 10^5 queries.

The union is a "Y" joining the three nodes (one arm may be empty), and each of its edges lies on exactly two of the three pairwise paths `src1–src2`, `src2–dest` and `dest–src1`. So the answer is half the sum of those three distances. A distance is `dist[a] + dist[b] - 2 * dist[lca(a, b)]`, where `dist` is the weight from the root, and binary lifting finds the lowest common ancestor in O(log n).

## Approach

1. Build `graph` for `n = edges.length + 1` nodes and run a BFS from node 0, recording each node's parent `up[0]`, its `depth` and its root distance `dist`.
2. Fill the lifting table: `up[j][v] = up[j - 1][up[j - 1][v]]` is the ancestor `2^j` levels above `v`.
3. `lca(a, b)`: lift the deeper node to the other's depth; if they meet, that node is the answer. Otherwise lift both by every power of two that keeps them apart; their parent is the ancestor.
4. `distance(a, b)` removes twice the ancestor's root distance from `dist[a] + dist[b]`.
5. For each query, add the three pairwise distances into `total` and return `total / 2`.

## Example 1, step by step

Rooted at 0, `dist = [0, 2, 5, 7, 6, 11]`. In query `[2, 3, 4]` every pair meets at node 1 (`dist[1] = 2`), so the distances are `5 + 7 - 4 = 8`, `7 + 6 - 4 = 9` and `6 + 5 - 4 = 7`; `total = 24` and the answer is `12` (edges 1–2, 1–3 and 1–4). Query `[0, 2, 5]` lies on one root path: the distances are `5`, `6` and `11`, `total = 22`, answer `11`. The result is `[12, 11]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((n + q) log n): the BFS is O(n), the table O(n log n), and each query runs three O(log n) ancestor searches.
- Space: O(n log n) for `up`, plus O(n) for the graph and the per-node arrays.

## Pitfalls

- `n` is not passed in; it is `edges.length + 1`.
- `distance(src1, dest) + distance(src2, dest)` counts the stretch the two paths share near `dest` twice.
- Use a BFS, not a recursive DFS: a path-shaped tree of 10^5 nodes overflows the call stack.
- The halving is exact, because the three distances always sum to twice the answer.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of nodes, `edges.length + 1` |
| `graph` | adjacency list of `[neighbour, weight]` pairs |
| `LOG` | number of levels in the lifting table |
| `up[j][v]` | the ancestor `2^j` levels above `v` (the root points to itself) |
| `depth`, `dist` | edges and total weight from node 0 to each node |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and its read position |
| `total` | sum of a query's three pairwise distances |

narration.2: The tree has one more node than it has edges.
narration.3: Build an adjacency list where each entry keeps the neighbour and the edge weight.
narration.9: Enough levels that any climb of up to n - 1 steps can be written as a sum of powers of two.
narration.10: up[j][v] will be the ancestor 2^j levels above v; the root points to itself.
narration.12: dist[v] will be the total edge weight on the path from node 0 to v.
narration.17: Breadth-first search from node 0 reaches every parent before its children.
narration.19: Look at each neighbour together with the weight of the edge leading to it.
narration.20: Skip the parent, which was reached already.
narration.22: Record the direct parent: the first level of the lifting table.
narration.23: A child is one edge deeper than its parent.
narration.24: Its root distance is the parent's plus the weight of the edge just crossed.
narration.29: Fill each higher level of the table from the level below it.
narration.31: A jump of 2^j levels is two jumps of 2^(j-1) levels.
narration.36: Make a the deeper of the two nodes.
narration.38: Lift a by 2^j levels whenever that keeps it no higher than b, until both are at the same depth.
narration.40: If b was an ancestor of a, the two now coincide.
narration.42: Jump both nodes only while they would still land on different ancestors.
narration.47: Both are now children of the lowest common ancestor, so return their parent.
narration.50: The path weight between a and b: both root distances minus twice the stretch above their common ancestor.
narration.53: Add the three pairwise distances; every edge of the smallest connecting subtree lies on exactly two of these paths.
narration.54: Halve the sum to get the weight of that subtree.
